claims.text: The initial HfNbTaTiZr alloy is a single-phase BCC solid solution.
The homogenized baseline has a near-random atomic distribution.
HfNbTaTiZr can develop local chemical short-range order because local stoichiometry can deviate from the global composition.
Controlled annealing can reproducibly produce different degrees of short-range order in HfNbTaTiZr.
Between 800 and 1200 °C, diffusion is sufficient for significant short-range order to develop.
The alloy remains in the relevant single-phase BCC state over the proposed 800–1200 °C test range.
Local lattice distortion influences dislocation mobility in chemically complex high-entropy alloys.
Increasing short-range order modifies local lattice distortions and dislocation core structures in HfNbTaTiZr.
Plasticity is primarily screw-dislocation dominated at lower temperatures.
Elevated temperature and increased short-range order drive a transition from screw-dominated to edge-dislocation-controlled plasticity in HfNbTaTiZr.
Increasing short-range order makes edge-dislocation motion easier.
Easier edge-dislocation motion caused by increased order decreases flow stress and yield strength.
Increasing short-range order changes the elastic moduli relative to the less-ordered baseline.
Increasing short-range order changes the thermal expansion coefficient relative to the less-ordered baseline.
In situ neutron diffraction can be used to determine elevated-temperature elastic moduli in a BCC refractory high-entropy alloy.
Changes in diffraction strain evolution and peak broadening can identify a shift in the dominant dislocation mechanism.
Below the proposed temperature range, insufficient atomic mobility may prevent development of the relevant short-range order.
Above the proposed temperature range, phase instability may produce a different controlling mechanism.
The experiment compares annealed, nominally more-ordered samples against homogenized baseline samples over 800–1200 °C.
Absence of statistically significant response differences or absence of diffraction evidence for a dislocation-mechanism shift would falsify the hypothesis.
